newsitem.title: ITALY: Accounting changes, lower interest bill help Italy.
newsitem.headline: Accounting changes, lower interest bill help Italy.

text.p: Italy's chances of shaping up for the single European currency have been given a boost by lower debt servicing costs and revised accounting methods, Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said on Monday.
Ciampi told a news conference that the closely watched ratio between Italy's public spending deficit and gross domestic product (GDP) fell to 6.8 percent last year from 6.97 percent in 1995.
To qualify for the 1999 launch of European economic and monetary union (EMU), the ratio must be sliced to three percent and Ciampi said the government was close to reaching this goal.
"Until a few months ago such a target seemed reckless. Now it is achievable, even if the path is very arduous and difficult," he told reporters.

The Treasury said the 1996 public administration deficit was 127.5 trillion lire ($76.8 billion), with a decision by the EU statistics office, Eurostat, to accept changes in state accouting, shaving 11.5 trillion lire off the original total.
Among other things, Eurostat has accepted an alteration in the way debt owed by state companies is booked along with a delay in writing down interest payments on postal bonds.
Further savings came from lower than expected interest costs, which are set to continue to fall this year.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government originally forecast it would spend 192.4 trillion lire in 1997 on servicing its debt mountain, but Ciampi said this estimate had now fallen to 184 trillion lire thanks to the recent fall in bond yields.
"We're not discounting any further fall (of yields). We are discounting a stabilisation at this level," he said.
Despite this reduction, the government is already planning fresh budgetary rigour to fulfil its EMU dream, just weeks after introducing 62.5 trillion lire of belt-tightening measures.

The final part of that package still has to be approved by parliament and the coalition announced on Monday it would hold a confidence motion in the lower house on Tuesday to force the measures past hundreds of opposition amendments.
Prodi relies on the hard-left Communist Refoundation for his majority in the lower house and is not expected to have serious difficulties winning the vote.
He might have a more difficult time persuading allies to swallow another dose of budgetary medicine and Refoundation has already said it will not back more tax hikes or spending cuts.

Refoundation's president, Armando Cossutta, was quoted as telling Corriere della Sera newspaper on Monday that his party might have to take difficult decisions over its support for Prodi in the near future.

The group, which last week openly questioned the future of EMU, is due to meet government representatives on Tuesday to discuss the planned mini-budget, which is expected to include up to 15 trillion lire of new deficit-cutting measures.
Ciampi warned there could be no delay to EMU. "It is essential to respect the Maastricht timetable," he said, adding: "Whoever talks about a delay obviously does not want EMU."
While Italy believes it can hit the three percent deficit/ GDP target, it stands no chance of meeting another key criteria -- a ratio between state debt and GDP of 60 percent or less.
In Italy, the ratio came in at 121 percent last year, but Ciampi said all state debt was covered by domestic savers with no debt overhang abroad. REUTER
